Could not determine whether the voice belonged to a man or a woman. Understood none of the words, but supposed the language was Spanish. This witness’s account of the condition of the room and the bodies agreed with the description we printed yesterday.

“Henri Duval, a neighbour and a silver-smith by occupation, declares that he belonged to the first party to enter the house. Supports Musèt’s evidence in its general particulars. Having forced their way in, they shut the door again to exclude the crowd, which gathered rapidly despite the late hour. In this witness’s opinion the shrill voice belonged to an Italian. Is certain that it was not French. Cannot affirm that a man was speaking; the voice might have been a woman’s. Has no knowledge of Italian. Could discern no words, but the intonation convinced him that the speaker was Italian. Was acquainted with Madame L. and her daughter and had often spoken with them both. Is sure the shrill voice belonged to neither of the deceased.

“——Odenheimer, restaurateur. Came forward voluntarily to give evidence. Since he speaks no French, his examination was conducted through an interpreter. Is a native of Amsterdam. Was passing the house when the shrieks occurred. They continued several minutes, perhaps ten. They were prolonged and loud, exceedingly dreadful and distressing. Joined those who entered the building. Confirmed the earlier evidence in every particular save one. Was certain that the shrill voice was a man’s, and that the man was French. Could not make out the words. They were loud, rapid, and irregular, seemingly uttered in both terror and anger. The voice was rough—harsh rather than shrill. Would not describe it as shrill. The gruff voice repeatedly said ‘sacré’ and ‘diable,’ and once ‘mon Dieu.’

“Jules Mignaud, banker with Mignaud et Fils, Rue Deloraine. Is Mignaud the elder. Madame L’Espanaye possessed some property. Opened an account at his bank in the spring of the year—eight years ago. Frequently paid in small amounts. Made no withdrawals until three days before her death, when she personally drew out 4000 francs. The amount was paid in gold, and a clerk accompanied the money home.

“Adolphe Le Bon, clerk employed by Mignaud et Fils, states that at about noon on the day mentioned he accompanied Madame L’Espanaye to her house, carrying the 4000 francs in two bags. When the door opened, Mademoiselle L. appeared and received one bag from him, while the old lady took the other.”

He mounted the spirited horse that had carried him to victory in Greece, and exhausted himself in numbing exertion, drowning the anguish of a troubled mind in bodily sensation.

Slowly he regained possession of himself; at last, like one recovering from poison, he raised his head above the mists of fever and passion into the quiet air of composed reflection. He considered what course would be best. First he was struck by the length of time during which madness, rather than any rational motive, had governed his conduct. A month had elapsed, and throughout it he had not visited Evadne. Her influence, bound to few of his heart’s lasting feelings, had weakened greatly. He was her slave no longer, nor her lover: he would never see her again, and by returning wholly to Perdita would earn her trust.

Yet even while he resolved upon this, imagination brought before him the Greek girl’s wretched dwelling, which noble and elevated principle had prevented her from exchanging for greater comfort. He remembered the splendour of her station and appearance when they first met; her life at Constantinople, surrounded by all the magnificence of the East; her present poverty, her daily labour, her solitude, her pale and hunger-worn cheek. His breast swelled with pity. He would visit her once more, contrive some means of restoring her to society and the privileges of her rank, and their parting would then follow naturally.

He reflected, too, how all through that long month he had shunned Perdita, fleeing her as he fled the reproaches of his conscience. Now, however, he was awake; all would be set right, and his future devotion would wipe away the memory of this single stain upon their peaceful life. The thought made him cheerful, and with sober resolution he determined the course he would follow. He recollected his promise to Perdita to attend that very evening, October the nineteenth, the anniversary of his election as Protector, a festival held in his honour. Let that festival foretell the happiness of years to come. First he would call upon Evadne. He would not linger, but he owed her an explanation, some amends for his lengthy absence without warning. Then he would return to Perdita, to the world he had neglected, to social obligations, the splendours of rank, and the pleasures of power.

After the scene described in the foregoing pages, Perdita had looked for a complete alteration in Raymond’s manner and behaviour. She had expected frank communication and a renewal of that affectionate companionship which had been the joy of her existence.

I walked quickly, and we soon reached my college. Then a thought struck me that made me shudder: the creature I had left in my rooms might still be there, alive and moving about. I dreaded seeing the monster, but feared even more that Henry might see him. I therefore begged him to wait a few minutes at the foot of the stairs and rushed up to my room. My hand had already reached the lock before I came to my senses. I paused, overcome by a cold tremor. Then I flung the door open, as children do when they expect a ghost to be waiting on the other side. Nothing appeared. Fearfully I stepped inside. The room was empty, and my bedroom too was free of its hideous guest. I could scarcely believe such good fortune had come to me, but once I was certain my enemy had really fled, I clapped my hands with delight and ran downstairs to Clerval.

We went up to my room, and a servant soon brought breakfast, but I could not control myself. More than happiness possessed me: my skin tingled with an excessive sensitivity, and my pulse raced. I could not stay in one place for even a moment. I jumped over chairs, clapped my hands, and laughed aloud. At first Clerval thought my unusual excitement came from pleasure at his arrival. But as he watched more closely, he noticed a wildness in my eyes he could not explain, and my loud, uncontrolled, mirthless laughter frightened and astonished him.

“My dear Victor,” he cried, “for God’s sake, what is wrong? Don’t laugh like that. You look so ill! What has brought this on?”

“Don’t ask me!” I cried, covering my eyes with my hands, for I thought I saw the dreaded apparition glide into the room. “He can tell you. Oh, save me! Save me!” I imagined the monster had seized me. I fought frantically, then collapsed in a fit.

Poor Clerval! What must he have felt? The reunion he had anticipated with such joy had turned so strangely bitter. But I did not witness his distress. I lay insensible and would not regain awareness for a very long time.

This marked the beginning of a nervous fever that kept me confined for several months. Throughout that time Henry alone nursed me. I later learned that, knowing my father was elderly and unfit for such a long journey, and knowing how deeply my illness would distress Elizabeth, he spared them that grief by concealing the severity of my condition.
